title: Production says v2.1.0. Prove what is actually running.
summary: During an incident, the only useful question is which commit is deployed. Stamp builds with a sha, verify a deployed artefact against the repository, and answer 'is my fix live yet' in one command.
mental_model: A version string is a label; a commit sha is an identity. Stamp the sha into every build and every deployment question — what is running, does it include this fix, does the artefact match the source — becomes a git query with a definite answer.

write.content:
#!/bin/sh
# Produce a build directory stamped with the exact commit it came from.
out="${1:-build}"
rm -rf "$out"
mkdir -p "$out"

git archive --format=tar HEAD | (cd "$out" && tar -xf -)

{
  echo "commit=$(git rev-parse HEAD)"
  echo "short=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)"
  echo "version=$(git describe --tags --always --dirty)"
  echo "tree=$(git rev-parse HEAD^{tree})"
} > "$out/BUILDINFO"

echo "built $out from $(git rev-parse --short HEAD)"

setup.run: git commit -q -m "feat: add the request handler"
git commit -q -a -m "fix: handle an empty request" --trailer "Refs: ABH-450"
git commit -q -a -m "feat: add trace flags" --trailer "Refs: ABH-460"

steps.title: Build an artefact stamped with its commit
steps.why: `git archive` exports the tree at a commit — no .git directory, no history, exactly what a deployment should contain. The BUILDINFO file records the sha, which is the piece that makes everything afterwards answerable.

actions.run: sh -c 'git checkout -q v2.1.0 && sh ci/build.sh ../deployed && git checkout -q main'

steps.expect: The application files plus a BUILDINFO naming the exact commit.

verify.label: the artefact is stamped with the release version

steps.title: Answer the first incident question
steps.why: 'What is running?' The sha in BUILDINFO resolves to a commit, a message and a date. This takes seconds and removes all guessing from the first five minutes of an incident.

steps.title: Answer the second: is my fix live?
steps.why: `git merge-base --is-ancestor <fix> <deployed>` is a yes/no answer, scriptable and unambiguous. It beats reading version numbers, which lie whenever someone re-tags or hotfixes.
commands: sh -c 'fix=$(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="handle an empty request"); dep=$(grep ^commit= ../deployed/BUILDINFO | cut -d= -f2); if git merge-base --is-ancestor $fix $dep; then echo "ABH-450 IS deployed"; else echo "ABH-450 is NOT deployed"; fi'

sh -c 'new=$(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="trace flags"); dep=$(grep ^commit= ../deployed/BUILDINFO | cut -d= -f2); if git merge-base --is-ancestor $new $dep; then echo "ABH-460 IS deployed"; else echo "ABH-460 is NOT deployed"; fi'
steps.expect: The fix is deployed; the trace feature is not.

verify.cmd: sh -c 'fix=$(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="handle an empty request"); dep=$(grep ^commit= ../deployed/BUILDINFO | cut -d= -f2); git merge-base --is-ancestor $fix $dep && echo yes'
verify.label: the fix is provably in the deployed commit

steps.title: Which release contains a given commit
steps.why: `tag --contains` answers it from the other direction: given a commit, which releases shipped it. This is the query for 'which customers have this fix'.
commands: sh -c 'git tag --contains $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="handle an empty request")'
sh -c 'git tag --contains $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="trace flags") || echo "no release contains it yet"'
steps.expect: v2.1.0 for the fix, nothing for the unreleased feature.

verify.cmd: sh -c 'git tag --contains $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="handle an empty request")'
verify.label: the fix shipped in v2.1.0

steps.title: Verify the artefact really matches the source
steps.why: The recorded tree sha is the strongest check available: recompute it from the repository and compare. If they differ, something modified the build after it left CI — which is exactly the kind of thing you want to detect during an incident.
commands: sh -c 'stamped=$(grep ^tree= ../deployed/BUILDINFO | cut -d= -f2); actual=$(git rev-parse v2.1.0^{tree}); if [ "$stamped" = "$actual" ]; then echo "artefact matches the tagged source"; else echo "MISMATCH"; fi'
steps.expect: A match — the deployed tree is the tagged tree.

verify.cmd: sh -c 'stamped=$(grep ^tree= ../deployed/BUILDINFO | cut -d= -f2); actual=$(git rev-parse v2.1.0^{tree}); test "$stamped" = "$actual" && echo match'
verify.label: the deployed artefact matches the source it claims to come from

steps.title: Catch a tampered deployment
steps.why: Someone edits a file on the server 'just to test something'. Comparing the actual files against the tree the artefact claims catches it immediately — a hand-edit on production is invisible to any version number.

actions.run:
sh -c 'printf "
# hand-edited on the server
DEBUG = True
" >> ../deployed/app.py'

commands: sh -c 'sha=$(grep ^commit= ../deployed/BUILDINFO | cut -d= -f2); git show $sha:app.py > /tmp/expected-app.py 2>/dev/null || git show $sha:app.py > expected-app.py; diff -q ../deployed/app.py expected-app.py && echo "matches" || echo "DEPLOYED FILE DIFFERS FROM ITS COMMIT"'
sh -c 'sha=$(grep ^commit= ../deployed/BUILDINFO | cut -d= -f2); git show $sha:app.py > expected-app.py; diff ../deployed/app.py expected-app.py | head -5'
steps.expect: A clear difference report naming the hand-edit.

verify.cmd: sh -c 'sha=$(grep ^commit= ../deployed/BUILDINFO | cut -d= -f2); git show $sha:app.py > expected-app.py; diff -q ../deployed/app.py expected-app.py >/dev/null && echo same || echo differs'
verify.label: the hand-edit on the server is detectable

steps.title: Make the stamp part of every build
steps.why: Commit the build script so every artefact carries its provenance. The whole scenario only works because one file records a sha — and that costs four lines in a build script.

actions.run: sh -c 'git commit -q -m "ci: stamp builds with their commit and tree" --allow-empty'

verify.label: the stamping build script is committed
a fresh build carries its own commit stamp
the deployed artefact records the exact release it came from
verify.hint: stamp git describe and git rev-parse output into the build

verify.cmd: sh -c 'fix=$(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="handle an empty request"); dep=$(grep ^commit= ../deployed/BUILDINFO | cut -d= -f2); git merge-base --is-ancestor $fix $dep && echo yes'
verify.label: you can prove whether a given fix is deployed
…and that the unreleased feature is in no release

verify.cmd: sh -c 'sha=$(grep ^commit= ../deployed/BUILDINFO | cut -d= -f2); git show $sha:app.py > /dev/null && echo readable'
verify.label: the deployed commit is resolvable in the repository
the stamping is part of the repository, not one runner's config

pitfalls: A version string is not an identity. Re-tagging, hotfixes and rebuilds all break the assumption that v2.1.0 means one specific tree — the sha does not.
`git archive` exports the tree with no history, which is what you want in an artefact. Shipping the `.git` directory into a container is a common and avoidable mistake.
`git describe --dirty` in a build script tells you immediately when someone built from an unclean checkout. Treat a `-dirty` artefact as unreleasable.
`git tag --contains` needs the tags fetched. In a shallow CI clone it silently returns nothing.
Recording the tree sha as well as the commit lets you detect post-build tampering, which the commit sha alone cannot.
cheatsheet: the identity to stamp into a build
the content identity, for tamper detection
a human-readable version that never fails
is this fix live: yes or no
compare a deployed file against its source
